Nothing slips past the lantern watch.
My lantern reveals more than shadows. Stay where I can see you.
Hold there. The lantern sees what the eye misses.
Mind the sparks, {className}. Good steel is the difference between a scar and a grave.
Forty years since I ground that eye and set it in his socket, and never a day paid. You want to hurt the Foreman, {className}? Aim for my work.
Rest now, spirit. I can return you to your body, but the crossing back leaves you weak.
Every rider walks in on two legs, {className}. I will not hand you the reins until you can sit the Valorsteed without kissing the dirt, and the Galecrest wind shows no mercy to a bad seat.
Out of the black trees at last. Breathe, stranger, the sun holds this side of the pass.
A hide is only as good as its tanning, {className}. The vats are ready when you are.
Fresh hides on the racks today, {className}. Scrape with the grain, never against it.
Welcome to the World Market, {className}. Buy from every adventurer in the realm, or set out your own wares and let coin find you.
The tide takes and the tide pays, {playerName}. I keep the tally of both: what the scuttlers pinch off the wrecks, and what honest hands carry back up this path.
The mere drinks the moonlight, {className}, and gives back the drowned. I have watched that gate for thirty nights, and tonight it is open.
Springs, sprockets, and sharp edges, {className}: the toolworks has whatever your hands lack.
Fresh bread, clean water, fair prices. What can I get you?
Fen took three of my lines this week. Fen never took a line in twenty years.
The chapel fell years ago. The dead beneath it did not notice, and so I stayed.
The breaks do not care that Gullhaven is small, {className}. We hold this shore, or there is no shore left to hold. Stand with us and I will not forget it.
Hold at the gate, {className}. Past those reeds, the fen does the killing for us.
Mind the benches, stranger. The snow keeps what it takes.
These lanes are the Gauntlet, {playerName}, and every adventurer the vale respects has run them. The lantern posts stay lit all night, so the lanes never close.
These forges cooled centuries ago, {className}, but their work still holds an edge.
Honor is the only coin I take, and the Warfare stores are mine to guard. Earn your rank on the field and I will armor you for the next one.
Mind your footing past the gate. The wind up here takes hats first and questions never.

Eastbrook takes all comers, friend. And for the unsteady, there is always the Proving Shore: the ferry bell down on the quay rings you across any day of the year, and its twin on the island rings you home.
Down the Steps and into the soft country. Mind where you plant your boots.
Snow behind you, gold ahead. Few walk the Goldmelt twice, so make the crossing count.
Feel that? Moonfleece on the loom. Warmer than any fire you have sat beside.
Mind the threads, {className}. A steady hand at the loom beats a strong one.
The Vale keeps a ledger of deeds, and I keep the ledger. Pick one charge for the week, see it through, and the purse is yours.
Come in, sit, there is cordial on the fire. Just keep a hand on anything iron: the gnomes are light-fingered of late.
A candle for every grave, and not one may go out. Not one, do you hear me?

Thieves hid their stolen gold all through my maze, and the shadows guard it now. Recover every coin purse. Avoid the guardians, or take a radiant wisp to banish them. Three lost lives return you to the entrance, but the purses you gathered remain safe.
There's bread in that bundle and a blanket without too many holes. Sit a moment, then we'll work out what brought your boat onto the rocks.

You're breathing, which puts you ahead of your luggage. Gather anything dry from that wreckage while I fetch a blanket. We can discuss your unusual choice of landing place once your teeth stop chattering.
That cord is cold enough to numb my fingers, yet the lantern was lit. I'll wrap it up for Eastbrook's priest, because I prefer my mysteries somewhere other than aboard my boat.

That beacon should have guided your boat clear of the rocks, not invited it onto them. Someone's been up there, and the rats along the path have started biting anything with a shadow. Have a look inside the lantern, but don't touch anything still burning.
Four healthy minnows, and not one signed complaint. We'll release them after I've checked their scales, which is more courtesy than they showed my last sandwich.
Loan Fishing Rod from the tackle rack
Shore Minnow caught at the jetty

Before we discuss fishing, you should understand that the fish consider themselves the injured party. Borrow my spare rod and catch a few minnows for the keep-net. Gently, please, because we're studying them rather than inviting them to supper.
Those will do nicely, and the gulls appear to have spared you. Now we can turn this pile into something people may confidently stand upon.
Shore Pine Logs placed on the timber rack

The cargo walkway has developed an interest in dropping people into the sea. Bring me four sound pine logs from the marked trees behind the hut. Leave the old nesting tree alone, unless you'd like to negotiate with thirty furious gulls.
That feels solid enough for a loaded handcart. It's a small repair, but someone will get home dry because you bothered.
Walkway Panels built at the ferry workbench

You've provided the wood, so now comes the business of convincing it to become a walkway. Use my bench and the nails in that chest. I've marked the gaps, although the sea showing through them is also a useful clue.
That is my hat, though the crab has improved its ventilation. Let him out once you are finished, because he has already suffered the indignity of being caught by breakfast.
Crab Pot baited with a Bait Herring
A crab has stolen my hat and now refuses to recognize my authority. Bait the pot beneath the jetty and retrieve it without hurting the little scoundrel. I want my hat back, not a diplomatic incident.
Welcome to Eastbrook, and thank you for bringing this safely. Jorren will find you a warm meal while I examine the cord, but I would like you to return afterward.

Eastbrook lies upriver, where people generally arrive through doors rather than shipwrecks. Take this wrapped cord to Brother Aldric at the chapel. Tell him I want an explanation, preferably one that doesn't involve buying a new ferry.
Then you have somewhere to begin, and people who know your name. Ivara has already sent word that the thread troubles her, though she cannot yet say why.
Beacon Thread Sample delivered to Ivara

A stranger needn't remain one for long here. Take a sample to Ivara, introduce yourself to Corren and Silven, and look at the work posted outside the inn. Eastbrook has room for another pair of willing hands.
That's clean metal, and I can work with it. A buckle won't earn a ballad, but it might keep the person wearing it alive.
Copper Ore mined in the eastern quarry
Copper Ingot smelted at the public furnace
The watch wants new breastplates, but half their existing straps won't hold a buckle. Bring me copper and smelt it cleanly. We can discuss glorious weapons after everyone can keep their armor on.
Both deliveries are accounted for, and neither customer has demanded my head. That is what I call a successful trading day.

Two labels were exchanged in a minor outbreak of administrative enthusiasm. Ivara needs her mortar, and Brunna needs her padded gloves. Please correct matters before either discovers an exciting new use for the other's order.
At least we'll have something for supper. That cord around the fence stake wasn't there when I planted, and I'd like to know who put it there.

The south bed grows turnips, while the north bed appears to be growing disappointment. Its soil is cold enough to keep butter, even at noon. Bring me good vegetables and a few bad roots before the whole patch decides it's winter.
The Cold End of the Garden
The wax draws warmth from whatever touches it, which explains Della's damaged crop. Removing it should help the bed recover, but please tell her to report anyone digging near her fence.

I've dug down beside that stake, and someone has tied knots around my roots. Knots, in a vegetable garden, as though the turnips might escape. Take the bindings to Ivara, along with balm for the plants we've had to disturb.
Nothing Good Tied to a Root
He heard someone counting after midnight, and this cloth matches the thread Fenlow sent. I would rather have found a thoughtless vandal than someone so careful.

Bertram found the flowers on three graves pushed into the soil, blossoms first. That is not one of our customs, nor a child's joke I recognize. Ask him what he saw and examine the graves without disturbing their occupants.
Thank you for treating them as people rather than obstacles. This lamp was never part of their burial, and I will find out who placed it there.

Bertram saw a man walking whom we buried together on Tuesday. I have checked the grave, and I fear there is no gentle explanation. Put the Gravestirred to rest and restore their name stones, because whatever moves them now must not take their names as well.
The soil has been drained of warmth, not poisoned. These bindings match the beacon thread, which means the trouble has been carried here by someone with hands.

The roots beside the burial ground have blackened, and even the foxes there have turned savage. Ivara believes the damage may tell us more than the graves alone. Take her herbs from the cold patches and anything tied among the roots.
These leaves still carry a lovely little hum. I'll use them gently, and perhaps the bridge will enjoy a quiet afternoon.

Those flowers beneath the bridge have been singing since dawn, and even a happy song becomes tiresome by the seventeenth verse. Lay a damp cloth over each patch before taking a leaf. You needn't pluck the whole choir to borrow a little music.
Please Do Not Pick the Choir
She came back arguing, which is usually a good sign. Thank you for taking the sacks as well, because she would have gone straight back for them.

Della took her handcart over the willow path after I warned her about the washout. I've found a wheel, but she shouted back when I called, so there's hope. Bring her and those seed sacks home before she attempts to repair the river.
Those flour prints are smaller than a mouse's, and something has eaten the word 'rent.' Whatever lives in that wall has already understood the expensive part of lodging.

Something in my pantry knocks three times whenever I serve supper. The guests say it's a ghost, but ghosts have never previously shown such an interest in dumplings. Find the cause before somebody starts selling tickets.
A cupboard spirit was tapping through the old speaking pipe to ask for food. It returned my key and offered three buttons for its room, so I believe we're making progress.
Asked Olvessa about the flour prints
Bread set on the Pantry Saucer

My pantry key has vanished, and the knocking has become rather impatient. Ask Olvessa what leaves tiny flour prints, then offer our visitor something from the kitchen. I'd prefer a negotiated settlement to dismantling my inn.
Three buyers used three different names, but all their orders went on the same cart. The destination was Old Kiln Lane, and I dislike being made useful without knowing to whom.

Someone needed wax, cord, and lamps for these workings, and those things pass through ordinary hands before reaching wicked ones. Silven may recognize the supplies. Ask what he sold, not what he believes, and let the records answer.
There are people below us tending lamps around an open pit, and something in that pit keeps trying to stand. I'll send word to Aldric while you keep those veils.

Neris has found where the supply cart left the road. Go with her while she follows the tracks, and watch the hedges when her eyes are on the ground. We need to know who is there before anyone attempts heroics.
That chest is yours, including everything you eventually manage to squeeze into it. Keep it safe until you've chosen a place, and don't let Silven convince you that hinges count as luxury fittings.
Vale Oak felled in the western coppice
Storage Chest built at Wenna's workbench
You keep bringing useful things back to town, and pockets have limits. Build yourself a chest while you consider where you'd like to live. You needn't own a house to begin making a home.
A Place for What You Keep
There you are, with room to work and enough floor left to walk across. Keep the table alongside your chest, because a useful home can begin with very little.
Vale Oak felled in the western coppice
Worktable tried on the Furnishing Practice Marker

A home ought to hold something you made, and somewhere to make the next thing. Build a worktable, then try arranging it in my demonstration cottage. No purchase required, and please resist testing the walls with an axe.
The watch will eat, and I shall amend my report to say 'persistent livestock.' Nobody needs to know how long I spent questioning the baker.

The patrol lunches have been stolen twice, and I will not have hungry recruits making decisions with spears. Clear the boars from the shelter and recover the baskets. For the record, I have withdrawn my earlier accusation of organized sabotage.
The pit is quiet, and those remains can finally be buried properly. These instructions look copied rather than composed, which means the people you stopped may not be the ones who began this.

Neris saw the dead rise when those lamps were lit and collapse when one went out. The people tending them attacked our messenger, so there can be no mistaking their intent. Stop the workings and bring back any instructions you find, because someone taught them this.

The original promise forbids keeping the dead in service to a crown, while this copy demands their obedience. An old cautionary verse calls such a ruler the Oathless King. The map places the promised resting ground beneath the Hollow Crypt.
Verse compared at the reading desk

This copied verse resembles a promise recorded in the Age of First Hearths, though someone has twisted its meaning. Fetch the old prayer boards from the loft and examine the map behind the painted panel. Our founders may have left us a warning worth hearing.
Good, because they'll look after the rest of us better with something warm inside them. I've kept a bowl for you, and that wasn't an invitation to argue.
Stew cooked at the inn hearth (2 Brook Trout, 3 Garden Carrots)

Everyone's been working late and pretending they aren't hungry. Help me make a few proper meals, then take them to the people too stubborn to stop. Terrible news can wait while somebody eats a carrot.

Fresh wax beneath the sealed doors is warning enough, and you were right to leave them shut. We will need experienced company before going farther. For tonight, Eastbrook has a watch on the road and one more reason to sleep.
Sealed Watch Warning delivered to Neris

The map leads to the Hollow Crypt, but finding a door does not oblige us to open it. Read the boundary stones and give Neris this warning. Stay outside the wicket, whatever you hear beyond it, and come back to me.
That should make the route safer for ordinary traffic. Good work, and thank you for returning without requiring a stretcher.

We've had reports of Culvert Rats troubling people at the town drainage ditch. Remove 5 of them and check your footing while you're there. I don't want a rescue operation attached to a routine patrol.
Then we can get something useful made today. You've earned your pay without needing to swing a hammer.

The workers at the eastern quarry need their hands for tools, not for beating off Quarry Burrowers. Clear 4 from the worksite. I'll pay for a safe shift rather than another tale about why the ore hasn't arrived.
I'll check the verge again on my next round. For now, the travelers behind you have a safer walk.
I've marked where Briarbitten Foxes are approaching the road at the northern root hedge. Deal with 4, but leave the healthy wildlife alone. We're protecting a path, not emptying the countryside.
That's a proper load, and the forge can use all of it. Come back another day when you need honest work.
Copper Ore gathered at the eastern quarry
I need 6 pieces of Copper Ore from the eastern quarry. Bring sound ore rather than a sack of interesting gravel. The furnace has enough opinions without being fed rubbish.
These will become something useful instead of remaining a sketch on my wall. I'll put the offcuts aside as well, because waste makes expensive furniture.
Alder felled in the brook grove
I've orders waiting for 4 Riverside Alder Logs, and the managed brook grove has trees marked for cutting. Leave the unmarked ones standing. Good carpentry begins before the wood reaches the bench.
These will become something useful instead of remaining a sketch on my wall. I'll put the offcuts aside as well, because waste makes expensive furniture.
Vale Oak felled in the western coppice
I've orders waiting for 4 Vale Oak Logs, and the western coppice has trees marked for cutting. Leave the unmarked ones standing. Good carpentry begins before the wood reaches the bench.
These are exactly what I needed. Thank you for bringing them promptly rather than letting them wilt beneath a collection of wolf teeth.
Silvermint gathered in the eastern meadow
I need 3 fresh Silvermint Sprigs from the eastern meadow. Take the healthy growth and leave enough for each plant to recover. A treatment gathered carelessly begins with an injury of its own.
Everything is signed for, so everybody knows whom to blame if it goes missing later. Your payment, happily, is considerably less complicated.

Please take 3 Hinge Bundles to Wenna at the carpenter's yard. The goods are paid for, properly labeled, and not yours to inspect for personal inspiration. Bring confirmation back, and we shall both enjoy the rare pleasure of an uncomplicated transaction.
A Receipt Is a Beautiful Thing
Everything is signed for, so everybody knows whom to blame if it goes missing later. Your payment, happily, is considerably less complicated.

Please take 3 Rivet Packets to Brunna at the forge. The goods are paid for, properly labeled, and not yours to inspect for personal inspiration. Bring confirmation back, and we shall both enjoy the rare pleasure of an uncomplicated transaction.
A Receipt Is a Beautiful Thing
Good, because the kitchen was already receiving complaints from imaginary future customers. There's something small for you on the counter, and this time you're permitted to eat it.

I've prepared 3 Bread Bundles for Neris. Take them straight to the northern lookout, because hungry people can turn a short delay into a lifelong grievance. Anything you smell along the way remains part of the delivery.
Good, because the kitchen was already receiving complaints from imaginary future customers. There's something small for you on the counter, and this time you're permitted to eat it.
Covered Stew Bowls delivered to Corren

I've prepared 3 Covered Stew Bowls for Corren. Take them straight to the training yard, because hungry people can turn a short delay into a lifelong grievance. Anything you smell along the way remains part of the delivery.
Then something will be tended that might otherwise have been neglected. Small journeys can do a surprising amount of good.
Dried Herb Packets delivered to Ivara
I've set aside 3 Dried Herb Packets for Ivara at the apothecary. Carry them gently and keep them dry. Things that grow deserve a little care even when they're wrapped in string.
Then something will be tended that might otherwise have been neglected. Small journeys can do a surprising amount of good.
Reed Mulch Bundles delivered to Della
I've set aside 3 Reed Mulch Bundles for Della at the riverside garden. Carry them gently and keep them dry. Things that grow deserve a little care even when they're wrapped in string.
That's a useful report, with places and observations rather than adjectives. I'll pass it to the next watch before they set out.
Check 3 Quay Inspection Posts along the riverside walk and report what you actually find. Do not substitute what a passing merchant claims his cousin saw. We have an entire council for that.
That's a useful report, with places and observations rather than adjectives. I'll pass it to the next watch before they set out.
Check 3 Road Checkposts along the south road and report what you actually find. Do not substitute what a passing merchant claims his cousin saw. We have an entire council for that.
I'll be able to follow that line of lights on tonight's round. So will everyone else who needs to reach home.

Several lamps along the Briar Gate circuit are running low. Take oil for 3 Watch Lanterns and check their shutters while you are there. Someone coming home late should be able to see the next safe place.
Excellent, because now I can arrange deliveries around the conditions rather than the gossip. Reliable information is a commodity I am occasionally willing to pay for.

I've heard three alarming accounts of the town's brook crossings, none from anyone who's visited them today. Inspect 3 Water-Level Gauges and bring me facts. Rumors are remarkably expensive when attached to a delivery schedule.

Gilt Measure seal, an old one, on a ship the harbor rolls say went down twice: once in a storm, and once again when someone tried to raise her. Either the sea is returning things, or someone wants us to think it is.

Crates have been washing up on the quay all morning, and they are dry inside. Wood that has been under the sea for years does not stay dry, {playerName}, and neither do I when I think about it too long. Bring me three of them and read the mark stenciled on the one the tide left by the bell.
Cargo From a Ship That Sank Twice
You heard it too. Bells, under the water, slow as a funeral. Well. The fish are excellent, and I intend to serve them before they hear anything else.
Skittish Harbor Fish caught off the town steps
Listened at the old jetty post

The fish below the town steps have gone nervous. Not shy, nervous, the way a cat goes nervous before a storm. Catch a few for my kitchen, then hold this old horn to the jetty post and tell me I am imagining the ringing.
Bells You Can Hear From the Steps
The wicket's ward has gone cold, and the key is warm. That is backwards in every way that matters. Very well. The crypt opens, and I will pray for whoever goes in first. That will be you.

We were right to leave the crypt shut. I would like that on record before I say the next part: it has to be opened now. Look at the Outer Wicket for me, then fetch the key from the sexton's lodge. Bring both your eyes and the key to Brother Aldric, in that order of importance.

A child's shoe, a wedding spoon, a letter to nobody. Each one is wet, and none of them has been near water. Someone is building homes out of what people have forgotten. I will write this down before I forget it as well.

Three houses stand along the causeway road this morning. I have walked that road every day for eleven years, and I would have noticed houses. Knock, look inside, and bring me anything left on the sills. Handle it gently; I suspect it remembers more than we do.
Solid as a promise, and quieter than most. Fenbridge walks dry tonight because you spent your afternoon on planks instead of glory. I will not forget it, which these days is saying something.
Boardwalk Planks cut at the bench

The boardwalk is sinking a hand's width a week, and the fog is not helping. Take my hatchet, fell the alders I have marked, and turn them into planks at the bench. Then replace the two spans that have started making noises a bridge should not make.
Good rice, fat eels, and not one memory of planting either. I have decided to be grateful rather than frightened. It is easier on the knees.
Paddy Eel taken from the traps

There is a harvest standing in my west paddy, and I do not remember sowing it. My hands do, apparently. Bundle what is ripe along the causeway bank, and empty my two eel traps before the eels eat the rest.
Five good hanks and a heath you can walk across without dancing. The cutters will sing about you, {playerName}. Badly, but they will sing.

Widows have spun over the heather east of the cuts, and my cutters walk into the webs every morning with a spade in one hand and a scream in the other. Clear them out for me. And bring back some of that silk: wound tight, it makes the best drying lines on the moor.
Quiet again, and the barrows only barrows. Tamsin says the moor is listening to something. I say it is listening to you now.

South of the Hearth Ring the old barrows have started to empty, and what climbs out walks the moor at dusk. They do not want our peat and they do not want our coin. They just walk, and anything in their way gets walked over. Lay them back down, {playerName}, gently if you can and firmly if you cannot.
Dry as a sermon, every brick. Ferncross will be warm tonight, and that is your doing.
Peat brick taken from a stack

The hounds have kept my cutters off the drying stacks for a week, and wet peat does not burn. Go down to the cuts and bring me a brick from each stack while the weather holds. The hounds will not thank you. Neither will your back.
No more tracks by the pony line this morning. The carts roll again. Thank you, {playerName}.
Prowlers have come up from the south heath and taken two of our ponies. A pony is a cart, and a cart is how the peat gets to market. Thin them out before they get bold enough to try the camp.
Wat sent you? Then he has worked out something is wrong before I have had time to write it down. Sit. There is more trouble in Panwick than there are pans, and I have a great many pans.
Speak with Odda Brinewell in Panwick

Panwick buys half my peat to boil their brine, and the Pan-Reeve has not sent a cart in a fortnight. Odda Brinewell does not miss a fortnight. Take the Applewold road south over the Saltmeads gate and find out what is keeping her. If it is trouble, she will be glad of you. If it is not, buy me some salt.
Ten fewer claws and I can finally rake a pan without counting my fingers after. You have the makings of a salter, {playerName}.
Scuttlers. Up out of the shallows and into the settling pans, snipping at anyone who bends over the brine. A boiler with no fingers is a boiler with no job. Go and teach them the pans are ours.
Six sacks, still dry. You would not believe how hard it is to find someone who can carry salt through a fight without spilling it.

Looters have been carrying off whole sacks from the drying sheds by night and camping west of the pans as if they owned the place. Salt is the only coin this town has. Get my sacks back, and if the looters object, let them object to you.
Clean, clear and sharp as a winter morning. Those will boil down into the best salt Panwick has made all season.

Now the scuttlers are gone, the pans need skimming before the brine sours. Go out to the Brine Pans and take a skim from each pan rim. Keep the scum out of it. If it is grey, it is wrong. If it is pink, run.
Greasy, thick and smelling of the downs. The crew will grumble about the smell for a week and then never take the gloves off.

Salters work with their hands in brine all day, and brine eats skin. The rams on the salt downs grow a fleece so greasy the brine slides right off it. Bring me some and the whole crew will have gloves by winter.
Thank you. I will have their names read in the square tonight, the ones I can still remember. Something sent them back to us. I want to know what.

The tide has started bringing in more than salt. Drowned men walk up out of the shallows east of the pans, still in salter aprons, still carrying rakes. Some of them I knew. Put them to rest, {playerName}. I cannot ask the town to do it.

Waterlogged, but legible. The last page is a tally of salt sold to a buyer with no name, paid in new coin, delivered to the Wychwold road. Salt does not go west, {playerName}. Nobody in the wold needs that much.
Every salter carries a tally book in a waxed pouch, and the drowned still wear theirs. One of them will say where they were working when the water took them. Find me a ledger that can still be read.
I could smell that from here. The pans will forgive you. Your boots may not.
Bloats have drifted onto the saltings east of town and they sour every pan they float near. Pop them, from a distance if you have any sense. I will not be helping with the washing afterwards.
Nan says you kept the scuttlers off the cart and only lost your temper once. From Nan, that is high praise.
Nan Saltash escorted to the Brine Pans

Nan Saltash takes the cart out to the Brine Pans for the morning skim, and twice this week the scuttlers have come up out of the water for her. Walk with her to the pans. If that ledger is right, I will need every sack we can make before somebody else comes asking for it.
Salt by the cartload? Out here? Nobody in the wold salts anything but the odd ham. Then somebody is buying it for something else, and I do not like the list of things that need that much salt.
Speak with Hesper Elmsley at Elmhallow

The ledger says the salt went west along the salt way, into the Wychwold. The Bracken Circle keeps a lodge at Elmhallow and Hesper Elmsley knows every cart that has rolled through the wold in thirty years. Take her the news, and ask her who in the wold is buying salt by the cartload.
The pack has gone quiet. My lads slept last night for the first time in a week, and only two clamps burned through. That is a good week, {playerName}.

A clamp has to be watched day and night or it burns through and you are left with ash. The wolves know it. They wait until a burner dozes and then they come for the lunch basket, and sometimes for the burner. Drive them off east of the lodge.
Good, sharp tusks. There is a kind of justice in pegging their own turf down with them.

The boars north of the lodge root up the turf we stack over the clamps, and a clamp with no turf is just a bonfire. Bring me some tusks. The Circle carves them into pegs for the turf, which the boars find very insulting.
They took, all four, though you say the smoke came out the wrong way at first. Into the ground instead of up. I will be asking Hesper about that.

Four of my clamps in the hollow went cold overnight. Not burned out: cold, with the wood still inside, like something drank the fire out of them. Take this firebrand down to the hollow and light them again. If they will not take, come back and tell me, and we will both pretend we are not worried.
Light on the wold floor again, and enough silk to bind the elm for a year. Thank you. Now I can show you what I have been afraid to look at alone.

Weavers have strung the elms south of here so thick that the light does not reach the floor. The Circle does not hurt the wold lightly, but a wood with no light is a dying wood. Cut them back, and bring me their silk. We weave it into the binding cords for the Knotted Elm.
Still now, all of them. They were facing the same way, east, toward the salt way. Whatever the salt is for, the dead under the elm know about it.

The old wold folk buried their dead among the roots of the Knotted Elm, so the tree would keep them. Now the tree is letting them go. They climb out of the roots and stand around the trunk as if they are waiting for someone. Lay them down again, {playerName}, before they decide who.

Cold, you say, and pulling toward the south-west. Toward the Tinmarch. Someone is taking salt and fire out of this country and sending it somewhere under the ground. The miners at Wheal Patience will know where the ground has been opened.

The elmroot dead wear knotted charms, the old binding the wold folk tied before the first hearth. Gather some from them, then go to the Knotted Elm and lay your hand on the trunk. If the binding still holds, you will feel it. If it does not, tell me what you felt instead.

The elm, pulling toward my moor. That is the second strange thing I have heard this week, and the first was a crew of strangers opening the old Blackadit without a licence. Sit down. I think we have the same problem.
Speak with Tobias Penhallow at Wheal Patience

Cross Tinners' Ford into the Tinmarch and find Captain Tobias Penhallow at Wheal Patience. He is a Gilt Measure man and he will want to argue about who pays for what. Let him. Then tell him the elm is pulling toward his moor, and watch his face.
The heaps have stopped twitching. My insurers will never know how close they came to paying out. Neither will my wife.
Diggers have burrowed into the spoil heaps east of camp, and a spoil heap full of tunnels is a spoil heap waiting to fall on somebody. Clear them out before my insurers hear about it.
I walked the north moor this morning and nothing followed me but my own shadow. You cannot assay peace of mind, but I would put a high value on it.

I walk the moor north of camp for samples, and lately something walks behind me. Stalkers, a whole family of them, and they have learned that an assayer with her nose in a rock does not look up. Make them reconsider.
Six lamps, and every one of them with the Wheal Patience mark scratched off and a pale sigil scratched on. Somebody is supplying those tunnelers, {playerName}. Tunnelers do not draw sigils.

Tunnelers came up from the Blackadit and stripped our lamp store bare. A miner with no lamp is a miner with no work, and the shift is waiting. They are camped by the old working south-east of here. Bring the lamps home.
Tin, mostly. And something else, bright as a struck spark and humming like a kettle. It is not ore. I do not know what it is, and that is not a sentence an assayer likes to say.
Ore sample taken from a spoil heap

The spoil heaps east of camp should be worthless: that is what spoil means. But my lamp flickers when I walk past them. Bring me a sample from each heap. Do not lick them. I am told people need telling.

Hold one to your ear. That hum is a hearth, {playerName}. A hearth with no fire, pulled up out of the ground and left to walk. Someone is drawing the old fires out of this country, and the stones are what is left over.

The hum in those samples leads to the Stannary Stones, west of camp. Living stone walks there now, tin and quartz grown legs, and it hums the same note. Break a few apart and bring me the cores. Carefully. I want to know what is singing.
They fought like people with somewhere to be. Whatever they are digging for, they think it is worth more than tin. That frightens me more than they did.

The Blackadit was sealed before my grandfather was born. It floods, it falls in and it eats lamps. Now a crew in pale coats has opened it and set the tunnelers to work for them. They are the Pale Accord, the same crew Coinwell chased off the chalk. Drive them out of my moor.

Salt to keep the deep workings dry, charcoal to keep them lit, and the hearths under the moor drawn up and sent on in sealed carts. No name at the bottom, only that pale sigil. This is bigger than one mine, {playerName}. I will send copies to Panwick, Elmhallow and the Gilt Measure's own house before the week is out.
A crew that organized carries orders. Find them. I want to know who signs for salt from Panwick, firebrands from the wold and the old fires from under my moor, and I want it in their own hand.
Three workings braced and my lads posted on the spoil heaps. The Accord will be back, but they will have to knock first. Wheal Patience will not forget it, {playerName}. Neither will I.

I cannot seal a mine my grandfather could not, but I can make it too much trouble to use. Take these pit props down to the three workings the Accord opened round the Blackadit and brace them shut. Nobody gets through a braced working without a week of work and a great deal of noise, and my lads will be listening.
Clay hearths, every one of them. The old moor folk buried their dead with a fire to carry. I will have Agnes take them back to the barrows at first light.

The walkers carry things out of the barrows with them: brooches, combs, little clay hearths no bigger than your thumb. Those belong in the ground with their owners. Bring me what they carry and I will see the keepers put it all back where it was.
Six clots, clean as poured honey. These gloves are stitched with the last batch, {playerName}: sap-stiffened, and warmer than they look.

The gilded stags bed down beneath my oldest trees, and the sap drips gold into their coats all night. Combed clots of it are the purest amber in the weald. Bring me six, {playerName}. The stags will not thank you, but they will not miss it either.
Ten, and the stores went untouched last night for the first time this season. The lamplighters send their thanks, {playerName}.

The gloam foxes have learned what the lantern stores are worth, {playerName}. Every dusk they slip the fences and carry off the tallow we press for the ferry lamps. Soft paws, softer conscience. Cull ten of them and the rest will remember to fear the town.
Quiet on the Goldmelt, and a traveler with snow in their hair to prove it. Sorrel keeps her watch too well to send idle word. Be welcome in Lanternmere, {playerName}. The lanterns burn for you.

You came over the Goldmelt, {playerName}, snow still on your boots. I keep this shrine so Lanternmere knows who walks in from the cold, and lately I have had little to report. Take the gold road down to the town, find Reeve Ottoline by the well, and tell her the pass is quiet.
All three, and still burning. Ferry lanterns do not go out in water, {playerName}. That is the point of them. What worries me is what pulled them loose.

Every ferry on the Mere carries a stern lantern, {playerName}, and three of my boats came back at dawn without theirs. The fog took them, or something in the fog did. They wash up along the east shore when the wind turns. Walk the shore road and bring my lanterns home.
The Reeve counts her carts, does she? Well, she can count them missing a while longer. Look at my rows, {playerName}. I have greater troubles than a late delivery.

Orchardist Pomeline keeps the Gilded Orchard on the west road, and her sap carts are three days overdue. The whole town runs on that amber sap, {playerName}: lamp resin, sweetening, the harvest ale. Walk the west road and find out what keeps her.
Four buckets back on their hooks and the rows gone quiet. You have a heavier hand with sprites than I do, {playerName}, and today I am glad of it.

Harvest sprites, {playerName}. They pry my sap-taps from the trunks for the sweetness inside and fling the buckets into the grass. Drive off eight of the little thieves and bring back four of my buckets, and the carts roll again.

The fog lifted off the Mere this morning, {playerName}, and the whole town saw it. The ferries will run the night crossing again, and every lantern on the water will burn in your name. Take this: it was dredged from the drowned jetty, and no one has better right to wear it.

The old ferrymen have a name they only say ashore: the Meredark, the first lurker, old as the lake and twice as patient. It rose once before, the year the drowned jetty went under, and it is rising now. At dusk it suns itself on the jetty ruin off the south shore, {playerName}. Take a friend, take two, and end it while it can still be ended.
Eight fewer shapes in the shallows, and the crossing ran on time today for the first time in a fortnight. But bold lurkers are driven lurkers, {playerName}. Something beneath the Mere is moving them.

Now I will tell you what I did not say in front of the town. The moorings were not slipped, they were bitten through. Mere lurkers, bolder every night, dragging at the ropes and the rudders. Put eight of them back under the water for good, {playerName}, before a ferryman goes with them.
This is no weapon I know. Look at how the plates fold. It may be a rare piece of armor, if it can be worn at all. Take it and try it on, {playerName}, but be careful.

I saw a rock fall out of the western sky, {playerName}. It struck the marsh wall and burst like a forge, far beyond the widow thicket. Go west, find what survived the explosion, and bring me anything that does not belong to this world.
Ten fewer knives in the dark. Take this: you have earned it.
A pack of cutthroats has made camp in the northwest hills. They have robbed three wagons this week. Drive them out: slay 10 Vale Bandits.

The ward parts like rotten rope. Ivara sent word that the Hearthpin fragment from the Hollow Crypt went warm at the very hour you brought me this stone. Whatever the Bastion keeps, the fragment knows it is there. The door stands open, and the dark below it is listening.

The Sunken Bastion, a knight's hold that drowned in the fen a century ago, is where Voss's chart points. The old warden rolls say it once kept a Hearthpin safe, and the bells everyone keeps hearing ring from inside it. The cult has warded its door with grave-stones. Bring me one of the ward stones, {playerName}, and I will unweave the seal.
Ah, fine bristly hides! These will fetch a good price.
Boar hide makes the finest travel packs, and the meadows northwest of town are crawling with the beasts. Bring me 5 Bristly Boar Hides and I will make it worth your time.
May they rest now, and may the Light forgive whatever woke them.

The old ruin on the northwest hill was a chapel once, and its yard a resting place. Something has stirred the dead from their sleep, the Gravestirred, as the old folk call them. Put them down and bring me a skull from each you lay to rest, {playerName}, eight in all, so I may speak the rites over them and grant the peace they were denied.
They burn blue and clean: the mountain remembers its old oath. With these I can unbind the gate for us alone.

The seal on the Sanctum was wrought with mountain-fire, and only mountain-fire will let us pass without tearing it wide open. The stormcrag elementals carry embers of that first forging in their cores. Bring me five Blessed Embers, {playerName}, for if the cult opens that gate first, they will not be careful, and the Wyrm will not wake gently.
Dead? Truly dead? Then the thicket is just trees again. The Light bless your blade, {playerName}.

You have seen the webs, now ask yourself what spins cables thick as a man's wrist. The wardens call her the Broodmother, and her clutch hangs over Widow Thicket like a second canopy. Smash 8 of her eggs and put the old mother down before the rest can hatch. Mind the clutch, some eggs will not go quietly.
You did what I could not bear to. The gatherers still sing in the south rings; because of you, they will keep singing.

The sporelings of the Gleaming Deep were gentle folk before the tear touched their rings. What the corruption takes, it does not give back. Grant the corrupted ones rest, {playerName}: ten of them, in the north of the Deep.
Ten crushers down. The war-camp is a body without a spine. Time to take the head.

Drogmar's war-camp squats in the eastern crags, and his crushers are the spine of it, each one worth three of my soldiers. Take companions; this is no errand for one blade. Break ten crushers and the warlord's muster breaks with them.
Twelve robes face-down in the mud. Every one carried the same pay, and not one would say whose. Now they know the fen watches back.

There, north past the third lake, where the mist never lifts. Grey robes, grey banners: Gravecallers, camped in the open like they already own the fen. This is no handful of fanatics, {playerName}. It is a cell of something larger, paid and supplied, and they have stopped hiding, which means they think they have already won. Prove them wrong. Cut down 12 of their cultists.
This script... I last saw its like in Morthen's grimoire, in Eastbrook. The same hand has guided every grave we have fought over, {playerName}.

The zealots move with purpose now, watches set and supplies counted, like soldiers before a siege. Cultists who organize are cultists taking orders, {playerName}. One of them is carrying written orders from below. Find the zealot who has them and bring the orders to me: I would know the hand that commands them.
Voss is dead, and in his coat was a chart of the Sunken Bastion, drawn by someone who has walked its drowned halls. The mist over the camp is already thinning. Now only the Bastion remains.

So a deacon of the Gravecallers stands at the heart of that camp, singing my drowned wardens up out of the lakes to serve him. Maren says he carries a chart he never lets out of his sight, and I want to know why. His hymn ends today. Take the camp road north, {playerName}, and put Deacon Voss in the ground, deep enough that nobody sings HIM back up.
That will push them back to the mud for a while. But a mudfin does not dig for pay unless someone taught it what pay is. Somebody out there is buying, and I mean to learn what.

The Deepfen mudfins kept to their shallows for twenty years. Now they swarm the east bank, dredging the lake bed day and night, and my wardens swear someone on the far shore pays them for what they haul up. I do not know who, and I do not like a marsh with a market in it. Cull 12 of the snappers and break their digging.
Ruthless and thorough. If this marsh ever dries out, there's warden's work waiting for you.

Aldric says those idols are cult-make, which means the mudfins are hauling the marsh's old evil up one armful at a time, and it all funnels through their reed-huts on the shallows. I will not have it washing onto my causeway. Take this firebottle, get right up against each hut, and burn the lot. Five should break their dredging for good.

The chapel yard grows quiet. You are ready for the words, {playerName}, but the Rite of Recall cannot be spoken in a warm chapel. It must be sung where the veil between life and death wears thin. I mean to carry the Tome north into the Mirefen Marsh. Follow me there, and we will finish this.

The Light does not rest in you quietly, {playerName}. I have watched you lay the dead to peace, and I believe you are ready for what few paladins are ever taught: the Rite of Recall, by which a fallen soul is called back to the living. Its words are kept in the Dawnbound Tome, here in my keeping, but a book is no blessing while the restless dead still walk this ground. Return 6 more Restless Bones to the earth, and I will begin to teach you.
Ten fewer blades in the dunes, and the muster fires burned lower last night. My sentries slept, which they have not done in a week. Well cut, {playerName}.

Look south off the palisade, {playerName}. Those fires in the dunes are not troll cookfires, they are ashbone musters, and every night there are more. The dead come up out of the bonefields with sand still in their teeth. Cut down ten raiders before they cut a road to my gate.
Three banners snapping in the hot wind, right where my glass can find them. With five warcallers silenced, whatever answers their call will come slower. You bought us time, {playerName}.

The ashbone muster at the old bonefield graves, {playerName}, and my patrols cannot read the dunes the way they read a wall. Kill five of their warcallers, the ones that scream the dead upright, and plant a warning banner on each muster ground so my sentries can mark it from the ridge.

Six brands, and one mark burned into every one of them. This is no raid muster, {playerName}. Every host in the dunes answers to the wargate below us, the trolls call it Orkadia, and no five soldiers I ever served with could break what drums behind that door. Perhaps five like you.

Every ashbone raider carries a war-brand, {playerName}: a scorched tally of the host it marches under. I have counted four hosts from this ridge, but guesses are not intelligence. Bring me six brands off the raiders and their warcallers, and I will give Brannoc the shape of the war that is coming.

The sky over the Drakemaw has been empty for two days, and now you walk through my gate with a matriarch's blood on your boots. Wyrmwatch has stood forty years on watch for exactly this, {playerName}. Take these pauldrons, mawscale, worked by our own smith. Wear them where the drakes can see.

The scales told it true, {playerName}. I climbed the rim at dawn and saw her on the crater floor: Cindraleth, the matriarch every emberwing in this sky was hatched under, gold as a coal about to catch. While she broods, the drakes grow bolder, and Wyrmwatch cannot fight dragons and the ashbone both. End her in her crater, then carry the word to Gatecaptain Brannoc. Do not go alone.
Look at the underside of this one, {playerName}: scorched in a spiral, and only one thing nests in circles. These drakes are brood-guards. Something in the Drakemaw is a mother.

When the wind turns off the Drakemaw, the emberwing drakes ride it over my camp low enough to count their teeth, {playerName}. They range farther every day, and something in that crater drives them. Bring me three of their scales. Scales remember heat, and I can read where a drake has been roosting by the burn.
Scorched black and every latch still holding. The smith gets his nails, the fletcher her strings, and you get the boots I was saving for whoever brought my crates back, {playerName}.

The last wagon burned, {playerName}, but iron-strapped crates do not burn through. Four of them are still lying scorched along the dunes road with a season of salt, nails, and bowstrings inside. Bring my stores home before the trolls work out how to open them.
Eight, and my drivers have stopped writing farewell letters before every run. The garrison eats because of you, {playerName}.

The dune trolls have learned the sound of a supply wagon, {playerName}. They hit the Cinder Dunes road three times this month, and the last driver walked in carrying nothing but the reins. Eight trolls off that road and my wagons roll again.

Brannoc sent you? Then my last runner never made it. Keep your voice down and sit, {playerName}. You see that gate below? Count the war-banners in front of it, and you will understand why I stopped writing things down.

Something is pulling the ashbone east, {playerName}, and I sent my best to learn what. Scout Yerrin has camped a month in the far dunes past Trollmoot, in sight of a gate nobody built in my lifetime. Her reports stopped ten days ago. Find her camp and get me her eyes.
Drogmar, dead in his own camp. The clans will scatter to the high passes: you have bought my wall a winter, {playerName}.

Warlord Drogmar took the Broodsworn's coin and swore the clans to the mountain's waking. He is the hammer they mean to swing at my wall, and when he slams the ground, {playerName}, do not be standing near him. Take your companions into the war-camp and end him, for Highwatch.
Each one you fell is a sailor set free. Some of them still carried Eastbrook harbor tokens in their pockets. Whoever drowned them is filling this fen like a tithing box, and the box is not yet full.

The dead walking out of the lakes are sailors, {playerName}. I know the cut of their coats: the crews of the ships that went missing off the harbor these past years, still hung with the weeds they died in. The sea took them, and something brought them here to stand guard in the fog. Return 12 of the Drowned Dead to their rest.
As I feared. These censers burned grave-ash, not incense. Someone consecrated that chapel to the drowning, and the rite is signed 'Voss.'

North of the widow lake stands a chapel that drowned with its congregation when the marsh rose. The dead there carry rusted censers, funerary ones, the kind swung at a Gravecaller rite. Gather 4 from the chapel yard and I will read what rite was sung over that water.

Pearls, knuckle-bones, a child's carved fish... grave-gifts, {playerName}. They are not raising the dead. They are dressing them, the way you dress a body for burial. The temple is a tomb that refuses to close.

The waders do not act alone. Among them walk the Drowned Votaries, the cult that sank with the temple, still in their rotted vestments, still singing the prayer from the shore-rocks. Silence eight of them, and bring me six of the offerings they carry. I would know what they mean to give their goddess.

The altar is dark, the water is still, and the moon over the tarn is only the moon. You drowned a goddess tonight, {playerName}, and the mountain will never know how close it came. Let the wardens of the shore-rocks rest easy at last.
Ysolei, Avatar of the Drowned Moon, slain

I have read the last of the rubbings, {playerName}, and I understand now what the cult drowned themselves to keep asleep. Ysolei, the Drowned Moon made flesh, coils on the altar at the temple's heart, and the stolen warmth of every life the mere took is pouring into her waking. When the moon stands full she rises, and the water rises with her: the tarn, the wall, the whole mountain under it. Gather the strongest you can find and put her back to sleep. For good, this time.
Look here: the leaves are curling in on themselves, every clipping the same. The garden is afraid, {playerName}. In a hundred years I have never once known it afraid.

You want to understand this garden? Then read it the way I do. The stags that graze the lawns grow the truest green: every leaf on them is a page. Bring me six fresh clippings from the topiary stags, {playerName}. They will not thank you for the pruning, but they will regrow. Everything here regrows.

I felt it, here, when he came apart. A hundred years of work, and you were right to end it. Take this mantle: I cut it for whoever proved stronger than my best. The court is only a fountain tonight, {playerName}, and the garden is only a garden. Perhaps now the Head Gardener and I can both sleep.

Now the truth, {playerName}. The bull at the heart of the maze was my masterwork: I shaped him to guard the Fountain Court, and for a hundred years he did. But the fear in the green has reached him, and he guards nothing now, he hunts. The maze feeds him whoever wanders in. I am too old to unmake him, and it must be unmaking, root and branch. Bring a friend, walk the maze to the court, and cut my bull down.
The Bull of the Fountain Court
Four rubbings, four sisters, and not one of them wept marble. The garden has taken your measure, {playerName}, and it did not find you wanting. Now I can send you where the trouble truly lives.

When the garden was young, the first gardeners raised four marble sisters to watch its quarters: one above the Rose Wilds, one on the pond walk east of the maze, one on the west lawn where the gnomes keep their warren, and one on the south lawn past the hedges. The maze grew up between them, and most folk never see all four. Walk the quarters, {playerName}, and press your palm to each sister. When the garden has looked you over from all four sides, it will open places it keeps from strangers.

Moved, did they. Pell reports that every week, and every week he is right. Forgive my eyes, {playerName}, I have not slept a whole night in years: someone has to watch the garden watch us. Welcome to Hedgewick.

The lawns past this gate have trimmed themselves for a hundred years, {playerName}, and lately they have started trimming visitors. Head Gardener Amaranth keeps the books in Hedgewick, up the road past the gate lawns. Tell her another traveler has come through, and tell her the hedges by the gate moved last night.
Three carts back and the pegs full again. Let the little devils sulk in their hedges: Hedgewick works these lawns too.

The shears were only the start, {playerName}. Last night the gnomes tipped our tool carts into the green, one out by their warren west of the maze, one clean across the garden on the pond walk, and scattered a hundred years of good iron in the grass. Drive off eight of the little devils and haul the spilled carts home.
Ten heaps of clippings where ten wolves stood. It should feel like gardening, {playerName}. Why does it feel like war?

Whoever shapes this garden has grown careless, or cruel. The wolf shapes out in the Rose Wilds were clipped for show, yet lately they hunt: green jaws, no bellies, and no reason ever to stop. Cut down ten topiary wolves, {playerName}, and let the lawns be lawns again for a while.
Six pairs, and my own among them, I would know the nick in the blade anywhere. Here, these gloves were knitted for pruning work. Warm hands make steady shears.

Every pair of shears in Hedgewick has walked off in a fortnight, {playerName}: off the pegs, out of locked sheds, one pair out of my own apron while I dozed. It is the hedge gnomes, the little groundskeepers who hate us walking their lawns. Get six pairs back before the whole hamlet is down to kitchen knives.

So the house finally sent someone. A hundred years I have walked these lawns, {playerName}, and the garden and I have an understanding: I trim what asks to be trimmed. Sit. The hedges can spare you an hour.
Find the gardener by the Lily Basin

I have kept the ledgers thirty years, {playerName}, and not slept properly for ten of them, because the sums will not close. Grass wants cutting and hedges want shaping, and nobody here does either, yet every dawn the garden stands trimmed. Lately the woodfolk swear they see an old man with a barrow on the far south lawns, past the maze by the Lily Basin. Find him. If he is real, I can finally sleep. If he is not, I suppose I never will.
The fragments hum like struck bells. The mountain is not angry, {playerName}... it is being disturbed.

Stormcrag has stood silent a thousand years, and now the very stones of it get up and walk. Elementals do not simply wake, {playerName}. Something beneath this mountain is turning in its sleep. Put twelve of them down so I may study what remains.

There, your first crop in your own hands. It keeps growing while you are away, and it never spoils. Your Harvest Journal (Shift+K, or the Farming row of your Professions window) lists every planted bed and its timer. Come back for seed whenever the beds call you, {playerName}.
Take this hoe and a pinch of vale wheat seed, {playerName}. Sow the seed in one of the beds beside me, then go about your business. Come back whenever you like and bring the crop in; I will be here.
Waterlogged, but whole. Poor drivers... the fen keeps what it catches, {playerName}. Remember that.

A caravan out of Eastbrook went into the mist three days back and never rang the gate bell. The wreck is strewn the whole length of the causeway: crates, casks, the lot, sinking slow. Salvage 5 loads of goods before the marsh finishes the job.
Aldric's seal, is it? Then you'll do. Three hamlets have gone into the fog this month, and my patrols keep coming back with fewer names than they left with. I need every blade that floats.

Villages along the northern marsh are vanishing into the fog, {playerName}: not burned, not raided, simply gone, with the paths still leading up to where they stood. Warden Fenwick has sounded the muster horn at Fenbridge, and Morthen's writings named a 'Fogbinder' in that same marsh. I do not believe in coincidence. Take the causeway north, pull the muster order from the gatepost, and present it to the Warden.

It still sings. Keep the ember: your hammer will need its voice. I have taught you one shaping of Forgebreaker. Use the ember to begin Requiem at the Forge. The ember and the shaping are spent only when your craft succeeds.

Varkhul kept an ember of the Last Spring at his heart. Recover it from him and use it to learn the shaping of Forgebreaker and begin Requiem at the Forge. This requires Weaponcrafting skill 125. You can also bring the ember to me to learn the shaping. His defeat on either difficulty will yield the ember while this task is active.

The causeway holds, and Tam still has breath enough to joke about the three-toll. Good. We are an island under siege, {playerName}, and every pair of hands that crosses that sandbar is a pair the breaks must get through before they reach my people. Welcome to Gullhaven.

You came over the Ferrywalk, {playerName}? Then you are the first in a week, and the Warden will want to look you over. Gullhaven sits up the shore road, past the drying racks nobody tends anymore. Tell Warden Coalfast the causeway still stands, and that Tam has not rung a three-toll today. Yet.
Bram! You brought him back to me whole, {playerName}. We both wept and neither of us is ashamed. Whatever the breaks take from this island next, they do not get my family. Not anymore.
Fisher Bram seen safely home to Gullhaven

My Bram took the boat out the morning the nets-break opened, and the sea threw him back somewhere past the Landing point. I heard him three nights ago, {playerName}, calling over the water, and I was too afraid to go. I am still too afraid. Please. His boat lies wrecked on the south shore. Walk him home to me.
Ten fewer, and the field hands are already arguing over who walks out first. It will not last, the breaks never rest long, but a town that eats is a town that holds.

East of town the grain rows have gone to wrack, and the wretches that came through the Riftfields break now pick them clean. My people cannot tend a field they cannot stand in, {playerName}. Cull ten of the wretches and give the farmers back their ground.
Moss in one hand and a quieter shoreline in the other. You have restocked my whole surgery, {playerName}. Do me the kindness of not becoming my next patient.

The salt moss that grows along the tideline is the best wound-packing I know, and the riftspawn have claimed every stretch of shore it grows on. They carry tufts of it snagged on their hides, of all things. Clear six of them off the east reaches, {playerName}, and pull me four good handfuls of moss from what they have trampled through.

The Warden sent you? Good. That means the town has finally started listening. Now be still a moment, {playerName}. There, under the wind, do you hear it? The cliffs are singing, and I do not like the tune.

There is a man who hears the breaks before they open. Riftwatch Ollun: a scholar, or a madman, and lately I cannot afford the difference. He keeps his vigil at the Watch Meadow, up the road southeast of town. Find him, {playerName}, and ask him what the island is about to do to us next.
Eight nights of circling, ended in one. The fires burn steadier already, or perhaps that is only my hands. Either way the meadow is mine again, and I can hear the island think.

The stalkers hunt the dark between the watchfires, and every night they circle my meadow a little closer. They are not mindless, {playerName}, they are patient, and patience is the one thing I cannot outlast. Kill eight and push the dark back to the cliffs it came through.
Salt-pitted and break-scarred, and it will hold an edge all the same. Here, I lined these grips myself. Steel for steel, {playerName}: it is the only trade the Farshore runs these days.

Every blade I hand out is one the sea gave back or one I pried off the dead, {playerName}. The wretches carry scrap through the breaks, hinges, hooks, broken sword-steel, magpie stuff, but it hammers out true. Bring me six pieces of their scavenged steel and the barricade line gets its teeth back.

Ollun sent word ahead: the singing stopped. My whole town heard the quiet, {playerName}, and half of them wept at the sound of nothing at all. Wear this mantle. The Farshore does not forget who held its shore.

Every song this island sings ends on the same low note, and it comes from the Sundered Cliffs. Something came through the great break there, {playerName}, something the cliffs themselves cracked open to admit, and it is still growing. If it walks north, no bell will matter. Take a friend, take two, and end it. Then tell Coalfast the tune has changed.
Three voices, three answers, carried clean over the water. Sleep in Gullhaven tonight, {playerName}, and know that if a bell wakes you, it will be by my hand and in good time.

Three watchbells stand the coast beyond my own: one on the Landing point, one on the south strand, one out by the Riftfields shore. If a rope has rotted or a clapper has been carried off, the town learns of a break when it is already in the streets. Walk the coast, {playerName}, and ring each bell once, so I know it still has a voice.
Six motes, still glowing. Look at them, {playerName}: they pulse in time with each other. The lights are not weather. They are a signal.

The wisps that drift these steps are shed by the lights themselves, and each carries a mote of the aurora in its heart. I need six to read what the sky is writing, {playerName}. The wisps do not fight back. Whether that makes the work easier or harder is between you and your conscience.
Still warm, every one. You have bought the lodge a whole winter of mercy, {playerName}.

A sledge of ember caches overturned on the tarn road in last night: iron kettles that hold a banked fire alive for a month. Three of them are still lying in the snow, {playerName}, and the lodge cannot spare what they hold. Bring the fire home.

When the wind dropped last night the whole village heard the silence where the Rimemane used to be. The Reach owes you a debt it will be years in paying, {playerName}. Wear this, and every door in Icemantle is open to you.

The howlers were not hunting when they came down the terraces. They were fleeing. A yeti has claimed the high ground, the mountain folk call it the Rimemane, and even the packs will not share a slope with it. It has to end, {playerName}, before winter drives it down to my walls. Bring a friend. Bring two.
Eight, and the dusk chorus is thinner for it. But howlers do not leave the peaks for nothing. Something up there moved them, and I fear it has a name.

You hear it at dusk, {playerName}: a howl off the Howling Terraces that is not the snowdrift packs. Bigger throats. The terrace howlers have come down from the peaks for the first time since my grandmother held this post, and they are what pushed the wolves onto my road. Cull eight and push them back.
Kaldra sent you? Then she is finally worried, and she is right to be. Sit, {playerName}. Watch the sky with me a while.

The aurora has burned green every night this month, and the old folk will not walk under it. One woman might know why: Veyla, the Aurorist. She camps alone on the Aurora Steps, southeast past the tarn. Find her camp, {playerName}, and hear what the lights have told her.
The night feels thinner already. Whatever wakes them is not done, but you have bought the Steps some quiet.

When the aurora burns this bright, the cold stands up and walks: rime elementals, frost given a will. They gather where the lights touch the benches, and they are wandering closer to my camp each night. Break eight of them apart, {playerName}, before one of them breaks me.
The girl is inside, wrapped in half my blankets and talking the stars out of the sky. You did a kind thing today, {playerName}. The Reach doesn't see many of those.
Apprentice Wren seen safely to the Aurora Steps

My apprentice Wren went out to walk the Goldmelt line two days ago and never came back. I found her tracks, she is holed up under the road markers northeast of the Aurora Steps, too scared of the wolves to move. I cannot leave the fen, {playerName}. Walk her to Veyla's camp on the Steps. She will be safe under the lights.
Maeve sent you? Ha. Eleven years and the woman still thinks the fen will eat me. Well... this year she might be right. Look at what it's done to my lines.

Old Brosk works the Shiverfen trapline west of here, and every week for eleven years he has sent a bundle of furs up with the wood sledge. Two weeks now, nothing. He is too stubborn to freeze and too careful to drown, {playerName}, so something else is wrong. Find his camp at the fen and see him breathing.
The pass holds, then. Einna sits that waycamp through storms that bury the road markers, and she has never once sent me idle news. Welcome to Icemantle, {playerName}.

Every soul who climbs out of the Drakelands passes my fire, {playerName}, and fewer climb every week. Warden Kaldra holds Icemantle up the north road. Tell her the pass is still open, and tell her a stranger walked it alone.
Four good traps back and the reeds gone quiet. You trap with a heavier hand than I do, {playerName}, but I cannot argue with the results.

Fen sprites, {playerName}. The little devils spring my traps for sport and scatter the iron in the reeds. Drive them off, eight should teach the rest, and gather up what is left of my traplines while you are out there.
Fur like this is the only argument winter listens to. Take these treads, they are lined with the last batch.

Firewood keeps a body alive, {playerName}, but wool will not turn this cold, only wolf-fur will. Six thick winter pelts off the snowdrift packs and I can line bedrolls for everyone the lodge shelters.
Ten fewer shadows between here and the tarn. The woodcutters are already arguing over who goes out first.

The snowdrift packs used to keep to the high benches. Now they cross the tarn road in daylight and my woodcutters will not leave the walls. Thin the packs, {playerName}, ten of them, and the road is a road again.
Six crews quieter and three crates high and dry. You salvage with a heavier hand than I do, {playerName}, but the ledger does not care. Half of this is yours by law, and by law I mean I say so.

Salvage law is simple, {playerName}: what the sea gives the beach is mine. The drowned deckhands disagree. They rise from their hulls and drag every crate I stack back below the tideline. Put six of them down for good, and while the beach is quiet, haul in three flotsam crates before the tide files its counterclaim.
Over the pass on foot, in this weather? Maren sends me few enough names, and fewer still walk in to answer for themselves. Welcome to Wickharbor, {playerName}. Close the inn door behind you.

You made the climb, {playerName}, so the wind has decided to keep you. Wickharbor sits east along the downs road, tucked in the lee of its cove. Harbormaster Odile counts every soul who comes over the pass, and she will want to count you. Tell her the Windway is still open.

Odile sent you all this way to see if the wind had taken me? Ha. Tell her the lamp burns and so do I. But since you have made the climb, {playerName}, stay a moment. The Beacon has work only a stranger seems fit to do.

Old Bram keeps the Beacon on the high head northeast of town, and he has not come down for his stores in two weeks. The lamp still burns, so he lives, but a man his age alone on that head in this wind, {playerName}. Climb the beacon road and see him standing.
Four points of light on the cliff road, right where they belong. From up here it looks like the coast has opened its eyes again. You have the makings of a keeper, {playerName}.

The Beacon is the great light, {playerName}, but it is the storm-lanterns that walk a night traveler down the cliff road above the Shear. Last night the gale doused every one of them, and that road in the dark is a long fall with a short ending. Take my striker and relight the four along the cliff.
Ten fewer shells on my road, and the pots came up full this morning. The potmen are calling you a good omen, {playerName}. In Wickharbor that is as warm as praise gets.

The shoal scuttlers have learned to climb the cliff road and crack our crab pots open on the stones, {playerName}. Half the catch gone this week, and one potman with a hand he will not be using for a month. Break ten of them and the rest will remember why they kept to the shoals.

Bram watches my shore from his tower now, does he? The old man is right to worry, {playerName}. The dead have been walking their own wrecks at night, and lately they have stopped caring whether the sun is up.

From this lamp room I can see the whole coast, {playerName}, and what I see in the north I do not like. Green lights walking the Wreckfields at low tide, hull by hull. One woman works that shore alone: Edda, the salvager. Follow the cliff road north past the Shear until the wrecks begin, and see that she still draws breath.

The beach went silent the moment it fell, {playerName}. First silence I have heard on this shore in ten years of working it. The crews are just bones now, resting bones. Take the mantle off the top of the hoard, it was always going to fit a living back better.

Now you know why the deckhands rise, {playerName}. Something wears the barnacled plate of the first wreck ever to break on this shore, and it wardens every hull on the beach like a graveyard it was hired to keep. It holds a hoard I have coveted for ten years and a crew I would rather see resting. End the Wreck Warden. Bring a friend, the dead keep good watch.
The lamp did not so much as gutter last night, first time in a month. The wind still hates us, {playerName}, but it has gone back to hating us fairly.

The gale wisps are the wind gone spiteful, {playerName}. They gather on the high downs by the Mirror Tarn, and every flame they find, they snuff, a lantern, a hearth, one day this lamp. Thirty-nine years I have kept the Beacon lit, and I will not lose it to weather with a grudge. Scatter eight of them.

Fleece like this is why the rams stand out there fat and smug in weather that kills men. The spinners will be at it by lamplight. Take these treads, {playerName}, they are lined from the last shearing.

My boat crews row into a gale that cuts through oilskin like paper, {playerName}. Only one thing turns this wind: the greasy wool off the moor rams, spun thick the Wickharbor way. The herds graze the Howling Downs west of town. Six good fleeces and every crew rows warm this season.
Look how they hold the light! No flame, no smoke, just the glow. The Hollow provides.

The veiled stags shed light where they graze, and their cast antlers hold it for years. Five of them, from the herds in the open glade at the heart of the valley, and my lanterns burn through the winter without oil. The stags need not be harmed, but they do not part with them easily.
A waking-prayer... to something they called the Drowned Moon. And below it, in a steadier hand: "It only sleeps." The water has been listening a long time, {playerName}.

Look there, {playerName}, under the surface, a stair of pale stone running down into the dark, and a gate of cold light at the head of it. The old wardens scratched warnings into the shore-rocks before the water took them. Take a rubbing of one for me; I would read what they feared before we go any closer.
Still warm. The Loremaster says the glow matches no flame he knows of. I say it is mountain trouble, and I say it kindly.

Caddis showed me a lump of wax taken off one of those tunnelers: it glows, {playerName}, and it is warm as a heartbeat. He wants more for study, and I want it off my requisition list. Bring back six lumps of the glowing wax.
All three delivered, and I hear Marlow cried. He always cries. Here is a basket of your own.
Basket left with Yara the herbalist

I fill a basket of sweets for an old friend in each town every Gourdlight Eve, and my knees are not what they were. Take them round for me, {playerName}: Cook Marlow in Eastbrook, Yara the herbalist in Fenbridge, and Loremaster Caddis up in Highwatch.
Black as a moonless field, and they smell of smoke already. The bonfire will be a sight. Thank you.

When Old Thatchgrin is pressed, he calls his crows down on whoever is beating at his straw. Their feathers burn green in a hearth, and I need three for tonight's bonfire. Find a fight at his patch, {playerName}, and pluck them from his crows.
Five round ones, and not a bite out of any. That is pie for the whole Vale. Here, for your trouble.

Old Thatchgrin's patch past Boar Meadow is fat with pumpkins, and half of them have rolled out past his straw where a careful soul can reach them. Bring me five, {playerName}. Stay wide of the old scarecrow himself. He counts every one.
Six stubs, cold as frost. Whoever lit them will have to try harder than that. Take this, and wash your hands.

Someone has been setting candles with green flames at the feet of our lamp posts. They burn without melting and they whisper when you turn your back. Snuff six of them for me, {playerName}, in any of the three towns, and bring me the stubs.
Morthen wrote to a 'Fogbinder' in the northern fen. The Pale Accord is not dead, {playerName}. It has merely been patient.

Morthen is dead, yet a question gnaws at me: an order that hid for a century does not spend itself on one village chapel. He kept a grimoire: his rites, his correspondence. If anything of it survives, it lies in the vestry of the ruined chapel above the crypt. Search the ruin and bring me whatever remains of his writings, {playerName}.
It is over. The dead of three lands may rest, the mountain sleeps unhaunted, and it is your name, {playerName}, that every bell from here to Eastbrook rings tonight.

There is no rite left to stop, {playerName}: only the Wyrm itself, half-woken in its hollow, gorged on the dead of the Vale and the fen. If it rises, the wall, the marsh, Eastbrook, everything we have defended falls in a single night. Take your companions into the Wyrm's Hollow and finish what we began in a chapel yard so long ago. The Light has carried you this far; carry it the rest of the way.
So the old devil is dead at last. The stable boy will sleep easier, and so will I.
There is one wolf no trap has held: Old Greyjaw. He has taken three hounds and a stable boy's arm. He prowls the deep woods north of the wolf runs. Bring me his fang.
The night market can open again. You have a customer for life, or at least a discount.
Duskwisps have started drifting in among my stalls after dark, {playerName}, and their chill spoils everything it touches. Thin them out for me: ten of them, wherever the veil has torn.
That tusk is long as my forearm! The mules are avenged, and Fenbridge owes you a round.

There's one troll the others won't dig beside: Grubjaw, the Glutton. He ate my last two pack-mules, harness and all, and my insurance man drowned years ago. He prowls the far eastern mounds, {playerName}. Bring me his tusk and I will outfit you proper.
Aldric's word reaches far. If the priest of the Vale is climbing the mountain himself, then it is as bad as I feared. Welcome to Highwatch, {playerName}.

Vael's last words have not left me, {playerName}: the Wyrm stirs beneath the peaks. Captain Thessaly commands the wall at Highwatch, at the head of the mountain road north. A summons stands posted at her gate: take it up, and tell her Brother Aldric is climbing the mountain behind you.

The whispering has stopped, and you came up carrying a piece of a Hearthpin, warm as a hand. When I held it I heard bells, {playerName}, slow and deep, ringing somewhere under the sea. The Vale's dead sleep at last. I fear the drowned do not.

The door we left shut stands open now, and Morthen the Gravecaller waits at the bottom of the Hollow Crypt, ringed by the elite dead he has raised. He is guarding something down there, something that has kept this Vale warm longer than any of us have been alive. He is far beyond any one hero: take four companions, no fewer. End him, and bring back whatever he was keeping.
So the First falls to the last. The herd is already calmer, do you feel it? You did the Hollow a kindness today, even if it does not look like one.

The second name is harder to say. Aurelhorn led these herds when my grandmother kept this lookout, and whatever woke in the Hollow woke him wrong. He tramples what he once warded, and the herd will not survive his madness. He roams the meadows near the old court roads. End him with mercy, {playerName}, and bring a friend to share the weight of it.
The shallows are just water again. I have watched that shell break better hunters than me, {playerName}. Not you.
